passage:
I'm Kunal, and the strangest part wasn't the questions, it was the silence after. I'd asked the temple committee why we do one ritual the way we do, and whether it had to be this way. Not to be rude. I wanted to know.

The next Sunday, aunties who used to press prasad into my hand looked past me. Talk stopped when I walked up. I stood by the shoe rack feeling like a stranger in a place I grew up in. Honestly, I was angry. I almost decided never to go back.

What changed things was Samir Uncle, who kept the temple library. He said, "Come, help me sort these books. Questions are fine here." And one friend from the youth group kept sitting next to me.

I don't agree with everyone there. But those two mattered more than any argument.

qa.a: Samir Uncle kept the temple library.

qa.q: How did Kunal feel standing by the shoe rack?
qa.a: Kunal felt like a stranger in a place Kunal grew up in, lonely and angry enough to nearly decide never to go back.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Kunal to hold on to a couple of people?
qa.a: Samir Uncle and the friend welcomed questions, so Kunal did not have to cut every tie in anger and could keep the community through people, not doctrine.

qa.q: How might the aunties see Kunal's questions?
qa.a: The aunties may hear the questions as a challenge to something they love, so they go quiet, which could be discomfort rather than a plan to shun Kunal.

grounding: People in the temple go cold when Kunal questions, Kunal feels lonely, and finds one elder and one peer who stay open.

passage: When I started asking questions at our temple study circle, it went quiet fast. I'm Ojas, and I was nineteen. I asked, politely I thought, why women in our circle weren't allowed to read certain texts aloud. The uncle who led the circle said, 'This is not the place for arguments.' The next week, two boys I'd grown up with stopped saving me a seat. At the festival, people nodded at my parents and not at me. I felt so lonely I almost walked out for good, and I wrote a long angry post that I thankfully never sent. What saved it was Nandini-aunty, who ran the temple library. She found me sulking by the shoe stand and said, 'Your question is an old one. Come on Thursday; I'll show you three saints who asked it.' I did. I still go on Thursdays. I don't win every argument. I just have one person there I can ask anything.

qa.q: What did Ojas feel when the boys stopped saving a seat?
qa.a: Ojas felt lonely and rejected, close to walking out for good.

qa.q: What turned things around for Ojas?
qa.a: Finding one open-minded elder, Nandini-aunty, and going to her Thursday sessions instead of cutting all ties.

qa.q: How might the uncle who led the circle have seen Ojas's question?
qa.a: The uncle seems to have seen it as an argument that threatened the circle, not as an honest question.

grounding: A spoken account of a temple circle going cold after honest questions, and finding one open-minded elder instead of cutting all ties in anger.

passage:
Sunday: At the youth group after mass in Mangaluru, Vikas asked why a loving God would shut out good people of other faiths. The leader closed the Bible and moved to the next topic. Afterwards, three friends went for ice cream without him.
The following Sunday: Nobody sat next to him in the pew. Vikas felt so alone he drafted a message to the group saying he was done with all of them. He didn't send it. He went home and lay on the floor.
Two weeks later: Damini, a quiet girl from the choir, stopped him on the church steps. 'I heard your question. I've wondered the same.' She said old Father Pinto, who taught at the seminary, loved hard questions. That Wednesday they went to see him together. Father Pinto poured tea and said, 'Good. Let's read.' Vikas walked home feeling less alone. He still went to the youth group, sometimes. He went to Father Pinto's every Wednesday.

qa.q: What did the leader do when Vikas asked his question?
qa.a: The leader closed the Bible and moved to the next topic.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling the following Sunday?
qa.a: Vikas felt lonely and hurt, enough to draft a message quitting the group.

qa.q: What choice worked better than cutting all ties?
qa.a: Finding open-minded people, Damini and Father Pinto, and meeting them weekly while still going to the group sometimes.

qa.q: What might Damini have felt when she heard Vikas's question?
qa.a: Damini felt a quiet recognition, having wondered the same, and wanted him to know he wasn't alone.

grounding: Shows a church youth group turning cold after a question, the loneliness it brings, and finding an open peer and elder instead of breaking away in anger.
